Cyclotomic generating functions, empty weighted complete intersections and positivity

Mona Gatzweiler M. GatzweilerFakultät für Mathematik, Universität Wien, Österreich Email address: mona.gatzweiler@univie.ac.at , Fabián Levicán-Santibáñez F. Levicán-SantibáñezFakultät für Mathematik, Universität Wien, Österreich Email address: fabian.levican@univie.ac.at and Atsuro Yoshida A. YoshidaFakultät für Mathematik, Universität Wien, Österreich Email address: atsuro.yoshida@univie.ac.at
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We give a sufficient combinatorial condition for the non-negativity of the coefficients of polynomial quotients of products of qq-integers, also known as cyclotomic generating functions (CGFs). This slightly extends work by Iano-Fletcher, Pizzato, Sano and Tasin, who studied this condition as a criterion for quasismoothness of complete intersections in weighted projective spaces. As a consequence, we solve a problem by Billey and Swanson, prove most cases of an unpublished conjecture by Stanton and most cases of two conjectures by Gatzweiler and Krattenthaler. We also study sufficient conditions given by structural properties of the division lattice.

1. Introduction

Let f⁡(q)f(q) be a non-zero polynomial with non-negative integer coefficients in the variable qq. Then, the polynomial f⁡(q)f(q) is called a cyclotomic generating function (CGF) if there exist α,β∈ℤ≥0\alpha,\beta\in\ZZ_{\geq 0} and a1,…,an,b1,…,bn∈ℤ+a_{1},\ldots,a_{n},b_{1},\ldots,b_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} such that

(1) f⁡(q)=α​qβ​∏i=1n[ai]q[bi]q=α​qβ​∏i=1n1−qai1−qbi,f(q)=\alpha q^{\beta}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{[a_{i}]_{q}}{[b_{i}]_{q}}=\alpha q^{\beta}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1-q^{a_{i}}}{1-q^{b_{i}}},

where [n]q=(1−qn)/(1−q)[n]_{q}=(1-q^{n})/(1-q) is a qq-integer. CGFs are of great significance in combinatorics as they are the generating functions of many combinatorial objects with respect to statistics on these objects. A prototypical example of such generating functions is the qq-binomial coefficient, being the generating function of integer partitions inside a k×(n−k)k\times(n-k) frame with respect to the area statistic:

(2) ∑λ⊂k×(n−l)q|λ|=(nk)q=∏i=1n(1−qi)∏i=1k(1−ql)​∏i=1n−k(1−qi).\sum_{\lambda\subset k\times(n-l)}q^{|\lambda|}=\binom{n}{k}_{q}=\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-q^{i})}{\prod_{i=1}^{k}(1-q^{l})\prod_{i=1}^{n-k}(1-q^{i})}.

For further reading, the paper [1] offers an excellent survey on CGFs from different perspectives and a long (but not exhaustive) list of sources of CGFs throughout combinatorics.

Considering the expression in (2), it is not a priori clear that the right-hand side is a polynomial with non-negative integer coefficients. In general, given a1,…,an,b1,…,bn∈ℤ+a_{1},\ldots,a_{n},b_{1},\ldots,b_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} and assuming that the quotient

(3) ∏i=1n1−qai∏i=1n1−qbi.\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{n}{1-q^{a_{i}}}}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}{1-q^{b_{i}}}}.

simplifies into a polynomial in qq, it is not easy to determine whether it has non-negative integer coefficients. Nevertheless, there are many known rational functions in the form of (3) that are polynomials with non-negative integer coefficients, as all CGFs are essentially of this form up to a constant and a power of qq.

The polynomiality and non-negativity of fractions of the form (3) have been extensively studied in the literature. For instance, in the unpublished note [12], Stanton posed the following conjecture related to fake Gaussian sequences.

Conjecture 1.1.

[12, Conjecture 1] Let 𝐚=(a1,…,an)\mathbf{a}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}) be a sequence of non-negative integers. If

(4) ∏i=1n(1−qm+i)ai∏i=1n(1−qi)ai.\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-q^{m+i})^{a_{i}}}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-q^{i})^{a_{i}}}.

is a polynomial for all non-negative integers mm and 𝐚\mathbf{a} is symmetric, then (4) has non-negative integer coefficients for all mm.

More recently, Gatzweiler and Krattenthaler [3] study the following conjecture.

Conjecture 1.2.

[3, Conjecture 1] Let n,k,l∈ℤ≥0n,k,l\in\ZZ_{\geq 0}. If

(5) (nk)q(nl)q=[l]q!​[n−l]q![k]q!​[n−k]q!=∏i=1l(1−qi)​∏i=1n−l(1−qi)∏i=1k(1−qi)​∏i=1n−k(1−qi)\frac{\binom{n}{k}_{q}}{\binom{n}{l}_{q}}=\frac{[l]_{q}![n-l]_{q}!}{[k]_{q}![n-k]_{q}!}=\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{l}(1-q^{i})\prod_{i=1}^{n-l}(1-q^{i})}{\prod_{i=1}^{k}(1-q^{i})\prod_{i=1}^{n-k}(1-q^{i})}

is a polynomial, then it has non-negative integer coefficients.

Note that in Conjecture 1.2 it suffices to consider the case where 1≤l<k≤n/21\leq l<k\leq n/2. In this case, (5) is equal to

(6) ∏i=n−k+1n−l(1−qi)∏i=l+1k(1−qi).\frac{\prod_{i=n-k+1}^{n-l}(1-q^{i})}{\prod_{i=l+1}^{k}(1-q^{i})}.

In [3], the authors prove Conjecture 1.2 for the cases in which l=k,k−1,k−2,k−3l=k,k-1,k-2,k-3 and l=0,1,2l=0,1,2 by direct arguments involving cyclotomic polynomials.

Furthermore, Gatzweiler and Krattenthaler claim that, in Conjecture 1.1, the conditions regarding the polynomiality of mm and the symmetry of 𝐚\mathbf{a} can be dropped. In other words:

Conjecture 1.3.

[3, Conjecture 4] Let m,nm,n be positive integers with m≥nm\geq n, and let 𝐚\mathbf{a} be a sequence of non-negative integers. If (4) is a polynomial in qq, then it has non-negative coefficients.

In this article, we study sufficient conditions for rational functions of the form (3) to have non-negative integer coefficients in the cases where these functions are polynomials. We classify our criteria into two categories: algebro-geometric and lattice-theoretic. The algebro-geometric point of view is particularly effective; we slightly extend ideas by [4] and [6] to give a necessary and sufficient combinatorial condition for the existence of empty complete intersections in weighted projective spaces. This condition involves a family of Frobenius coin problems. It can be stated as follows:

Proposition 1.4 (Proposition 3.3).

Let a1,…,an,b1,…,bn∈ℤ+a_{1},\ldots,a_{n},b_{1},\ldots,b_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}. Let A=[ai]i=1,…,nA=[a_{i}]_{i=1,\ldots,n} and B=[bi]i=1,…,nB=[b_{i}]_{i=1,\ldots,n} be the corresponding multisets. Then, the following are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    There exists a regular sequence of homogeneous elements f1,…,fnf_{1},\ldots,f_{n} of maximal length with deg⁡(fi)=ai\deg(f_{i})=a_{i} in ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] with deg⁡(xi)=bi\deg(x_{i})=b_{i}. In other words, there exists an empty weighted complete intersection Xa1,…,an⊂ℙ⁡(b1,…,bn)X_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}}\subset\mathbb{P}(b_{1},\ldots,b_{n}).

  2. 2.

    For every subset of indices I⊆{1,…,n}I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}, the inequality #⁡(A​∩¯​⟨set⁡(BI)⟩semigroup)≥#​I\#(A~\overline{\cap}~\langle\toset(B_{I})\rangle_{\text{semigroup}})\geq\#I holds.

The reader is referred to Sections 2 and 3 for definitions and notation.

In [1], the authors define the HSOP monoid (HSOP stands for homogeneous system of parameters) as the set of CGFs that are Hilbert series of the quotient of ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] by a regular sequence of homogeneous elements f1,…,fnf_{1},\ldots,f_{n} of maximal length. They note that this set is a monoid. They propose the following:

Problem 1.5.

[1, Problem 60] Besides identifying a specific homogeneous system of parameters in a graded ring, how can one test membership in the HSOP monoid?

Proposition 1.4 (Proposition 3.3) gives a solution to Problem 1.5. The following is our main theorem, which provides a more practical sufficient condition.

Theorem 1.6 (Theorem 3.9).

Let a1,…,an,b1,…,bn∈ℤ+a_{1},\ldots,a_{n},b_{1},\ldots,b_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} with ai≤ai+1a_{i}\leq a_{i+1} and bi≤bi+1b_{i}\leq b_{i+1} for all i=1,…,n−1i=1,\ldots,n-1. Let A=[ai]i=1,…,nA=[a_{i}]_{i=1,\ldots,n} and B=[bi]i=1,…,nB=[b_{i}]_{i=1,\ldots,n} be the corresponding multisets. Assume that

∏i=1n1−qai1−qbi∈ℤ⁡[q].\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1-q^{a_{i}}}{1-q^{b_{i}}}\in\mathbb{Z}[q].

Assume further that

2​bn​⌊bn−12⌋−b1<a1.2b_{n}\left\lfloor\frac{b_{n-1}}{2}\right\rfloor-b_{1}<a_{1}.

Then, for every subset of indices I⊆{1,…,n}I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}, #⁡(A​∩¯​⟨set⁡(BI)⟩semigroup)≥#​I\#(A~\overline{\cap}~\langle\toset(B_{I})\rangle_{\text{semigroup}})\geq\#I. In particular,

∏i=1n1−qai1−qbi∈ℤ≥0​[q].\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1-q^{a_{i}}}{1-q^{b_{i}}}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}[q].

Applying this theorem to Conjecture 1.2, we obtain the following corollary.

Corollary 1.7 (Corollary 3.10).

Conjecture 1.2 is true if

2​k​⌊k−12⌋+k−l<n.2k\left\lfloor\frac{k-1}{2}\right\rfloor+k-l<n.

In particular, it is true if n≥k2n\geq k^{2}. Hence, it is true except perhaps for finitely many choices of l,nl,n for each choice of kk.

Furthermore, applying Theorem 3.9 to Conjecture 1.3, we obtain the following corollary.

Corollary 1.8 (Corollary 3.11).

Conjectures 1.1 and 1.3 are true if

2​n​⌊n2⌋−2<m.2n\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor-2<m.

In particular, they are true if m≥n2m\geq n^{2}. Hence, they are true except perhaps for finitely many choices of mm for each choice of nn.

From the lattice-theoretic point of view, we give sufficient criteria involving lower order ideals of the division lattice of positive integers (Proposition 4.1). However, we also note that lattice-theoretic conditions cannot be necessary for a rational function of the form (3) that is a polynomial to have non-negative coefficients. This is because certain CGFs are non-negative for analytic reasons; we mention relations to Poincaré multipliers and normal distributions.

2. Preliminaries

In this section we summarise preliminaries that will be used in the rest of the paper. We recall basic facts about cyclotomic polynomials, CGFs, the Frobenius coin problem and regular sequences. We also introduce notation for multisets.

The symbols ℤ+\mathbb{Z}_{+} and ℤ≥0\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} will always denote the positive and non-negative integers, respectively.

2.1. Multisets

We use square brackets [[ and ]] for multisets (e.g., [1,1,2,3][1,1,2,3]).

For a multiset SS, we write set⁡(S)\toset(S) for its underlying set, so set⁡([1,1,2,3])={1,2,3}\toset([1,1,2,3])=\{1,2,3\}. We also write #​S\#S for its multiset cardinality, so #⁡[1,1,2,3]=4\#[1,1,2,3]=4.

For an indexed multiset S=[s1,…,sn]S=[s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}] and a subset of indices I⊆{1,…,n}I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}, we define SI≔[si:i∈I]S_{I}\coloneq[s_{i}:i\in I].

For two multisets S1S_{1} and S2S_{2}, we write S1⊎S2S_{1}\uplus S_{2} or ⨄i=12Si\biguplus_{i=1}^{2}S_{i} for multiset or additive union (so [1,1,2,3]=[1,2]⊎[1,3][1,1,2,3]=[1,2]\uplus[1,3]) and S1∖S2S_{1}\setminus S_{2} for multiset difference (so [1,3]=[1,1,2,3]∖[1,2,4][1,3]=[1,1,2,3]\setminus[1,2,4]).

Finally, for a multiset SS and a set S′S^{\prime}, we define S∩¯S′≔[s∈S:s∈S′]S~\overline{\cap}~S^{\prime}\coloneq[s\in S:s\in S^{\prime}]. For example, [1,1,2]=[1,1,2,3]​∩¯​{1,2}[1,1,2]=[1,1,2,3]~\overline{\cap}~\{1,2\}.

2.2. Cyclotomic polynomials

For n∈ℤ+n\in\ZZ_{+}, define D(n)≔{d:d∣n}D(n)\coloneq\{d:d\mid n\}, P(n)={p prime:p∣n}P(n)=\{p\text{ prime}:p\mid n\} and ω⁡(n)≔#​P​(n)\omega(n)\coloneq\#P(n). We write rad⁡(n)\rad(n) for the radical of nn.

Let n∈ℤ+n\in\ZZ_{+}. The cyclotomic polynomial Φn​(q)\Phi_{n}(q) of order nn is defined by

Φn​(q)≔∏1≤k≤ngcd⁡(n,k)=1(q−e2​π​i​k/n).\Phi_{n}(q)\coloneq\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq k\leq n\\ \gcd(n,k)=1\end{subarray}}(q-e^{2\pi ik/n}).

For f⁡(q)=a0+a1​x+⋯+an​xn∈ℤ⁡[q]f(q)=a_{0}+a_{1}x+\cdots+a_{n}x^{n}\in\mathbb{Z}[q], define A⁡(n)=maxi=1,…,n⁡|ai|A(n)=\max_{i=1,\ldots,n}|a_{i}|. The polynomial f⁡(q)f(q) is called flat if |A⁡(n)|≤1|A(n)|\leq 1. Furthermore, it is well-known that

1−qn=∏d|nΦd​(q).1-q^{n}=\prod_{d|n}\Phi_{d}(q).

We are also going to use the following standard properties of cyclotomic polynomials.

Proposition 2.1.
  1. 1.

    Φn​(q)\Phi_{n}(q) is flat if nn has at most two distinct odd prime factors [5]. In particular, it is flat if ω⁡(n)≤2\omega(n)\leq 2.

  2. 2.

    Φn​(q)\Phi_{n}(q) has at least one negative coefficient if ω⁡(n)≥2\omega(n)\geq 2.

  3. 3.

    Φp​(q)=1−qp1−q=1+q+q2+⋯+qp−1\Phi_{p}(q)=\frac{1-q^{p}}{1-q}=1+q+q^{2}+\cdots+q^{p-1} if pp prime.

  4. 4.

    Φn​(q)=Φrad⁡(n)​(qn/rad⁡(n))\Phi_{n}(q)=\Phi_{\rad(n)}(q^{n/\rad(n)}).

  5. 5.

    Φn​(q)​Φn​p​(q)=Φn​(qp)\Phi_{n}(q)\Phi_{np}(q)=\Phi_{n}(q^{p}) if pp prime and p∤np\nmid n.

  6. 6.

    Φn​p​(q)=Φn​(qp)\Phi_{np}(q)=\Phi_{n}(q^{p}) if pp prime and p|np\mid n.

2.3. Cyclotomic generating functions (CGFs)

In [1], the authors give several equivalent definitions for a CGF. We list the ones that will be useful to us.

Theorem 2.2.

[1, Theorem 1] Let f⁡(q)f(q) be a non-zero polynomial with non-negative integer coefficients in the variable qq. Then, the following are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    f⁡(q)f(q) is a CGF.

  2. 2.

    (Rational form.) f⁡(q)f(q) is of the form (1).

  3. 3.

    (Complex form.) The complex roots of f⁡(q)f(q) are all either roots of unity or zero.

  4. 4.

    (Cyclotomic form.) The polynomial f⁡(q)f(q) can be written as a positive integer times a product of cyclotomic polynomials and factors of qq.

The next lemma follows immediately from the definition in terms of cyclotomic polynomials.

Lemma 2.3.

Let a1,…,am,b1,…,bn⊂ℤ+a_{1},\ldots,a_{m},b_{1},\ldots,b_{n}\subset\mathbb{Z}_{+} with m≥nm\geq n. The following are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    The quotient

    ∏i=1m1−qai∏j=1n1−qbi∈ℤ⁡[q].\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{m}1-q^{a_{i}}}{\prod_{j=1}^{n}1-q^{b_{i}}}\in\mathbb{Z}[q].
  2. 2.

    The inclusion

    ⨄i=1nD⁡(bi)⊆⨄i=1mD⁡(ai)\biguplus_{i=1}^{n}D(b_{i})\subseteq\biguplus_{i=1}^{m}D(a_{i})

    as multisets holds.

2.4. The Frobenius coin problem

Let S={s1,…,sn}⊂ℤ+S=\{s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}\}\subset\mathbb{Z}_{+} with si<si+1s_{i}<s_{i+1} for all i=1,…,n−1i=1,\ldots,n-1. The numerical semigroup generated by SS is

⟨S⟩semigroup≔{c1​s1+c2​s2+⋯+cn​sn:ci∈ℤ≥0}.\langle S\rangle_{\text{semigroup}}\coloneq\{c_{1}s_{1}+c_{2}s_{2}+\cdots+c_{n}s_{n}:c_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\}.

Numerical semigroups are intimately related to the Frobenius coin problem, which informally is about finding the monetary amounts that we can make with coins of given denominations. The classical formulation is actually to find the largest monetary amount that we cannot make with these coins, but we will use the following stronger formulation.

Problem 2.4 (Frobenius coin problem).

Assume gcd⁡(S)=1\gcd(S)=1. Determine ℤ∩⟨S⟩semigroup\mathbb{Z}\cap\langle S\rangle_{\text{semigroup}}. In other words, the problem is to find all integers that are representable as a linear combination of elements of SS with non-negative integer coefficients.

If gcd⁡(S)=1\gcd(S)=1, the quantity

F⁡(S)≔max⁡{i∈ℤ:i∉⟨S⟩semigroup}F(S)\coloneq\max\{i\in\mathbb{Z}:i\notin\langle S\rangle_{\text{semigroup}}\}

is finite and is called the Frobenius number of SS. In general, giving a simple closed formula for F⁡(S)F(S) is only possible if #​S=2\#S=2. This being said, there are many known non-strict upper bounds for F⁡(S)F(S). One of the most famous such bounds is given by the following proposition.

Proposition 2.5 (Selmer’s bound [10]).

If gcd⁡(S)=1\gcd(S)=1, then

F⁡(S)≤2​sn−1​⌊s1n⌋−s1.F(S)\leq 2s_{n-1}\left\lfloor\frac{s_{1}}{n}\right\rfloor-s_{1}.

If gcd⁡(S)≠1\gcd(S)\neq 1, we will find it useful to consider the quantity F⁡(S/gcd⁡(S))F(S/\gcd(S)) instead.

For an excellent book about the Frobenius coin problem, see [9].

2.5. Regular sequences

Let R≔ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]R\coloneq\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] be the ring of polynomials in the variables xix_{i} with coefficients in ℂ\mathbb{C}. Let f1,…,fm∈Rf_{1},\ldots,f_{m}\in R be a sequence of non-zero homogeneous polynomials. Then, the polynomials f1,…,fmf_{1},\ldots,f_{m} form a regular sequence of homogeneous elements if fif_{i} is not a zero-divisor in R/(f1,…,fi−1)R/(f_{1},\ldots,f_{i-1}) for all i=1,…,mi=1,\ldots,m. While regular sequences are defined for any commutative ring, since RR is Cohen-Macaulay, the definition is equivalent to requiring that dim(V⁡(f1,…,fm))=n−m\dim(V(f_{1},\ldots,f_{m}))=n-m. For a very thorough treatment of these topics, see [2].

3. The algebro-geometric point of view

In this section we give a necessary and sufficient combinatorial condition for the existence of regular sequences on graded polynomial rings with given sequences of degrees. This condition is given in terms of a family of Frobenius coin problems. To do so, we rely heavily on ideas in [4, Theorem 8.7] and [6, Proposition 3.1], who first introduced this as a criterion for quasismoothness of weighted complete intersections (WPIs), which is the corresponding object in projective algebraic geometry. We use [11, Corollary 3.3] to translate this into a sufficient condition for the non-negativity of cyclotomic generating functions (CGFs). As a consequence, we solve Problem 1.5 and prove most cases of Conjectures 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3.

We work over ℂ\mathbb{C}. For a sequence of degrees b1,…,bn∈ℤ+b_{1},\ldots,b_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, we set ℙ≔ℙ⁡(b1,…,bn)\mathbb{P}\coloneq\mathbb{P}(b_{1},\ldots,b_{n}) to be the weighted projective space Proj⁡ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]\Proj~\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] with deg⁡(xi)=bi\deg(x_{i})=b_{i}. The space ℙ\mathbb{P} is a projective toric variety of dimension n−1n-1.

For each degree a∈ℤ+a\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, the reflexive rank-one sheaf 𝒪ℙ​(a)\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(a) has a corresponding complete linear system

|𝒪ℙ(a)|≔ℙ(H0(ℙ,𝒪ℙ(a)))=ℙ({p∈ℂ[x1,…,xn]:p homogeneous,deg(p)=a}).|\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(a)|\coloneq\mathbb{P}(H^{0}(\mathbb{P},\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(a)))=\mathbb{P}(\{p\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]:p\text{ homogeneous},~\deg(p)=a\}).

The base locus of |𝒪ℙ​(a)||\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(a)| is the set of points in ℙ\mathbb{P} where all elements of |𝒪ℙ​(a)||\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(a)| vanish.

For a subset of indices I⊆{1,…,n}I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}, we define the closed stratum

ΠI={x∈ℙ:i∉I⟹xi=0}≅ℙ(bi:i∈I),\Pi_{I}=\{x\in\mathbb{P}:i\notin I\implies x_{i}=0\}\cong\mathbb{P}(b_{i}:i\in I),

and the open toric stratum

ΠI∘={x∈ℙ:i∈I⇔xi≠0}.\Pi_{I}^{\circ}=\{x\in\mathbb{P}:i\in I\iff x_{i}\neq 0\}.
Remark 3.1.

Usually one works with well-formed weighted projective spaces, meaning that

gcd⁡(b1,…,bi−1,bi+1,…,bn)=1\gcd(b_{1},\ldots,b_{i-1},b_{i+1},\ldots,b_{n})=1

for all i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n. Every weighted projective space is isomorphic to a well-formed one; the weights of the latter are calculated via a reduction algorithm. However, this reduction algorithm does not generally preserve the sheaves 𝒪ℙ​(a)\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(a). Indeed, the first step involves the natural isomorphism

f:ℙ=ℙ⁡(b1,…,bn)→∼ℙ′≔ℙ⁡(b1/d,…,bn/d),f:\mathbb{P}=\mathbb{P}(b_{1},\ldots,b_{n})\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb{P}^{\prime}\coloneq\mathbb{P}(b_{1}/d,\ldots,b_{n}/d),

where d=gcd⁡(b1,…,bn)d=\gcd(b_{1},\ldots,b_{n}). Even though

f∗​𝒪ℙ′​(a)≅𝒪ℙ​(d​a)f^{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{\prime}}(a)\cong\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(da)

for all a∈ℤ+a\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, if a<da<d and a∈⟨b1/d,…,bn/d⟩semigroupa\in\langle b_{1}/d,\ldots,b_{n}/d\rangle_{\text{semigroup}}, we have that dim(|𝒪ℙ′​(a)|)≥0\dim(|\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{\prime}}(a)|)\geq 0 but |𝒪ℙ​(a)|=∅|\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(a)|=\emptyset. Since the toric strata ΠI\Pi_{I} may not be well-formed, we work with general weighted projective spaces and take special care in making sure that our complete linear systems are not empty.

For another sequence of degrees a1,…,am∈ℤ+a_{1},\ldots,a_{m}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} with m≤nm\leq n, a weighted complete intersection (WCI) Xa1,…,am⊂ℙX_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{m}}\subset\mathbb{P} is the vanishing set of a regular sequence of homogeneous elements f1,…,fm∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]f_{1},\ldots,f_{m}\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] with deg⁡(fi)=ai\deg(f_{i})=a_{i}. In other words,

Xa1,…,am=Proj⁡ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn](f1,…,fm)=V⁡(f1,…,fm)X_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{m}}=\Proj~\frac{\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]}{(f_{1},\ldots,f_{m})}=V(f_{1},\ldots,f_{m})

is a projective variety of dimension n−m−1n-m-1. If m=nm=n, then Xa1,…,anX_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}} is an empty weighted complete intersection, but

ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn](f1,…,fn)\frac{\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]}{(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n})}

is an Artinian ring and a finite-dimensional vector space.

We note that (Q1) in [6, Proposition 3.1] can easily be translated into a combinatorial statement involving a family of Frobenius coin problems. However, while they characterise general quasismooth WCIs in well-formed weighted projective spaces, we use similar ideas to characterise the existence of at least one WCI in general weighted projective spaces. It turns out that doing this is relatively straightforward, and that (Q2) in [6, Proposition 3.1] is redundant if both degree sequences are of the same length (i.e., if m=nm=n). This gives a solution to Problem 1.5.

Since Theorem 3.9 is quite general, it is very likely that Proposition 3.3 can be used to prove even more cases of the aforementioned conjectures by using specific properties of the multisets AA and BB. For example, Conjecture 1.2 involves intervals, which, along with the polinomiality, may force the elements of AA to be much larger than the elements of BB.

4. The lattice-theoretic and analytic points of view

In this section we give more sufficient conditions for the non-negativity of cyclotomic generating functions (CGFs). This time, the conditions arise from structural properties of the division lattice (ℤ≥0,∣)(\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0},\mid). We will also see that such conditions cannot be necessary, since CGFs are often non-negative for analytic reasons. In particular, we will briefly discuss Poincaré multipliers and asymptotic normality.

By abuse of notation, we will sometimes denote (ℤ≥0,∣)(\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0},\mid) by ℤ≥0\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. It is well-known that it is a distributive lattice with the meet operation being the GCD and the join operation being the LCM. Furthermore, ≺\prec will denote a covering relation.

Proposition 4.1.

Let a1,…,am,b1,…,bn∈ℤ+a_{1},\ldots,a_{m},b_{1},\ldots,b_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} with m≥nm\geq n. Let A=[ai]i=1,…,m,B=[bi]i=1,…,nA=[a_{i}]_{i=1,\ldots,m},B=[b_{i}]_{i=1,\ldots,n} be the corresponding multisets. Assume that the quotient

The following are sufficient conditions for (7) to have non-negative coefficients:

  1. 1.

    The multiset

    The multiset Δ\Delta is a disjoint multiset union of sets DkD_{k} such that, for each kk, either

    1. a.

      ω⁡(Dk)⊂{0,1}\omega(D_{k})\subset\{0,1\}, or

    2. b.

      Dk={d,d′}D_{k}=\{d,d^{\prime}\}, where d≺d′d\prec d^{\prime} and ω⁡(d)≤1\omega(d)\leq 1.

  3. 3.

    There exists a bijection f:{1,…,n}→{1,…,m}f:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{1,\ldots,m\} such that D⁡(bj)⊆D⁡(af⁡(j))D(b_{j})\subseteq D(a_{f(j)}) (equivalently, bj|af⁡(j)b_{j}|a_{f(j)}) for all j∈{1,…,n}j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}. In this case, the corresponding local quotients are non-negative and flat.

The following are sufficient conditions for the local quotients in (7) to be flat:

  1. i.

    The multiset Δ\Delta is a disjoint multiset union of sets DkD_{k} such that, for each kk, either

    1. a.

    2. b.

      Dk={d,d′}D_{k}=\{d,d^{\prime}\}, where d≺d′d\prec d^{\prime} and ω⁡(d)≤2\omega(d)\leq 2.

All of these conditions also have a corresponding “local” version which is generally more useful in examples, because then it is possible to use different criteria for different local quotients.

Proof.

Example 4.2.

Even if m=nm=n, the quotient (7) may be a polynomial with at least one negative coefficient. For example,

(1−q105)​(1−q3)​(1−q5)​(1−q7)(1−q35)​(1−q21)​(1−q15)​(1−q)=Φ105​(q)\frac{(1-q^{105})(1-q^{3})(1-q^{5})(1-q^{7})}{(1-q^{35})(1-q^{21})(1-q^{15})(1-q)}=\Phi_{105}(q)

which famously has a negative coefficient of −2-2.

Remark 4.3.

In Proposition 4.1 3, there may exist a well-defined function f:{1,…,n}→{1,…,m}f:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{1,\ldots,m\} such that D⁡(bj)⊆D⁡(af⁡(j))D(b_{j})\subseteq D(a_{f(j)}) for all j∈{1,…,n}j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, but ff may not be a bijection, even if m=nm=n. Indeed, in Example 4.5, 11 and 33 must both map to 11 and 22 must map to 22 (because b1,b3|a1b_{1},b_{3}\mid a_{1} and b2|a2b_{2}\mid a_{2}), so 33 must have empty preimage (because bi∤a3b_{i}\nmid a_{3} for all i=1,2,3i=1,2,3).

In general, however, if the quotient (7) is a polynomial, there always exists a well-defined function ff with the property mentioned above, simply because, for all j∈{1,…,n}j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, the cyclotomic polynomial Φbj\Phi_{b_{j}} is a factor of 1−qai1-q^{a_{i}} for some i∈{1,…,m}i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}, which implies that bj|aib_{j}\mid a_{i}.

Example 4.4.

Consider the polynomial quotient:

(1−q60)​(1−q66)​(1−q72)(1−q10)​(1−q11)​(1−q12).\frac{(1-q^{60})(1-q^{66})(1-q^{72})}{(1-q^{10})(1-q^{11})(1-q^{12})}.

The second local quotient is equal to:

Φ2​Φ3​Φ2⋅3​Φ2⋅11​Φ3⋅11​Φ2⋅3⋅11.\Phi_{2}\Phi_{3}\Phi_{2\cdot 3}\Phi_{2\cdot 11}\Phi_{3\cdot 11}\Phi_{2\cdot 3\cdot 11}.

We could apply Proposition 4.1 1 to deduce local non-negativity, with the triplets

(D⁡(11),2,1) and (D⁡(2⋅11),3,1),(D(11),2,1)\quad\text{ and }\quad(D(2\cdot 11),3,1),

and similarly for the other local quotients.

We could also apply Proposition 4.1 3 to deduce global non-negativity, since

10∣60,11∣66,12∣72.10\mid 60,\quad 11\mid 66,\quad 12\mid 72.

If at least one of the conditions in Proposition 4.1 were generally true for the sequences

(ai)i=1,…,k−l=(l+1,l+2,…,k) and (bj)i=1,…,k−l=(n−k+1,n−k+2,n−k),(a_{i})_{i=1,\ldots,k-l}=(l+1,l+2,\ldots,k)\quad\text{ and }\quad(b_{j})_{i=1,\ldots,k-l}=(n-k+1,n-k+2,n-k),

Conjecture 1.2 would follow. Unfortunately, this is not the case, as the following example shows:

Example 4.5.

Consider the polynomial quotient:

(27117)q(27114)q=(1−q255)​(1−q256)​(1−q257)(1−q15)​(1−q16)​(1−q17)=Φ3⋅17​Φ5⋅17​Φ3⋅5⋅17​Φ25​Φ26​Φ27​Φ28​Φ257,\frac{\binom{271}{17}_{q}}{\binom{271}{14}_{q}}=\frac{(1-q^{255})(1-q^{256})(1-q^{257})}{(1-q^{15})(1-q^{16})(1-q^{17})}=\Phi_{3\cdot 17}\Phi_{5\cdot 17}\Phi_{3\cdot 5\cdot 17}\Phi_{2^{5}}\Phi_{2^{6}}\Phi_{2^{7}}\Phi_{2^{8}}\Phi_{257},

which, as can be seen by using e.g. SageMath [13], has non-negative coefficients (!) This is remarkable, since Φ3⋅17​Φ5⋅17​Φ3⋅5⋅17\Phi_{3\cdot 17}\Phi_{5\cdot 17}\Phi_{3\cdot 5\cdot 17} has negative coefficients (it is also flat by Proposition 4.1 i). In other words, the non-negativity does not come from a geometric sum or a low-omega argument such as those used in the proof of Proposition 4.1, but from a genuine interaction between the different local quotients. SageMath also tells us that Φ25​Φ26​Φ27​Φ28​Φ257\Phi_{2^{5}}\Phi_{2^{6}}\Phi_{2^{7}}\Phi_{2^{8}}\Phi_{257} has a normal-like coefficient distribution.

Theorem 4.6.

[7] Let f∈ℝ⁡[x]f\in\mathbb{R}[x] be a polynomial. The following are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    f⁡(x)>0f(x)>0 for all x≥0x\geq 0.

  2. 2.

    There exists g∈ℝ⁡[x]g\in\mathbb{R}[x] monic such that f​gfg has only non-negative coefficients. The polynomial gg is called a Poincaré multiplier.

Theorem 4.7.

[8] Let f∈ℝ⁡[x]f\in\mathbb{R}[x] be a polynomial such that f⁡(x)>0f(x)>0 for all x≥0x\geq 0. Then, there exists k∈ℤ+k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} such that f⁡(x)​(1+x)kf(x)(1+x)^{k} has only non-negative coefficients.

Corollary 4.8.

Theorem 4.7 applies to finite products of cyclotomic polynomials Φni\Phi_{n_{i}} with ni≠1n_{i}\neq 1 for all ii.

Proof.

If ni≠1n_{i}\neq 1, it is well-known that Φni​(0)=1\Phi_{n_{i}}(0)=1. Also, Φni\Phi_{n_{i}} has all of its roots in the unit circle. Since ni≠1n_{i}\neq 1, 11 is not a root. Therefore, Φni​(x)>0\Phi_{n_{i}}(x)>0 for all x≥0x\geq 0. ∎

Note that (1+x)k(1+x)^{k} also has a normal-like coefficient distribution. Therefore, it seems that multiplying by polynomials with normal-like coefficient distributions makes the product have non-negative coefficients. This is the analytic reason for the non-negativity of certain CGFs. In this direction, results about asymptotic normality of coefficient distributions of products of cyclotomic polynomials, such as those in [1], could help find more such necessary or sufficient criteria.
